claims.claim: The shared board holds the working state of one case, alive for minutes, in an ordinary object in memory, and is not memory.
A board field can have one owner, and a value two agents can both set is one neither can trust.
An agent gets a write tool only for the fields it owns, and a write to someone else's field is refused.
Reading the board is injection into each agent's context, while writing is a tool bound to one agent.
Chapter 4's stores keep what should outlive a run, persisting to disk (SQLite and Chroma to files, Neo4j to a server).
Which store a memory goes in is decided by what will be asked of it later: KeyValue by name, Records filtered/counted, Journal by words/resemblance, Graph walked.
The board is for what agents need while working one case together, while a store is for what must still be there in a later run.
LangGraph waits with interrupt(), and resuming re-runs the node from its first line.
In LangGraph, the node returns a Wait object that tells the system which field to wait on.
claims.why: LangGraph waits with interrupt(), whereas returning a Wait object is how the case file ends a step and waits.

claims.claim: In the case file, a Wait object names the field, its owner, and the step that continues, and writing that field starts the next step.
A side effect before the interrupt in the same node, such as an email, happens twice in LangGraph but only once in the case file.
LangGraph matches answers to interrupt() calls by position, so a deploy that reorders them swaps the answers.
The case file stores each answer in its approver's own field, preventing mismatch from reordering.
Command(resume=...) accepts whoever answers, recording the wrong person's approval as the right person's.
The case file refuses unauthorized answers and keeps waiting.
In both, durability stops at the workflow, meaning external state like payments in another process's memory is not persisted.
The case file does not support rewinding/forking, parallel steps, streaming, or a server out of the box.
